questions.stem: What is a Vision Transformer (ViT) in Computer Vision, and how does it process images differently from a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)?
options: ViT splits images into patches but processes them with fixed local convolution filters, expanding receptive fields through deeper stages. CNNs first convert entire images into a token sequence so that attention scores can connect distant regions directly.

ViT splits an image into patches, projects them into tokens, and uses Transformer self-attention to mix information across regions. CNNs instead build features with sliding local filters, although deeper layers can also learn broader context.

ViT keeps every pixel separate and applies self-attention to individual color channels, while CNNs combine nearby pixels into patch tokens before feature extraction. The main difference is whether labels are assigned before or after image processing.

ViT converts patches into tokens and uses their physical order to decide which regions can exchange information. CNNs also convert image patches into tokens but use attention restricted to neighboring pixels instead of learned convolution filters.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A Vision Transformer (ViT) is a neural network that treats an image as a sequence of small patches. Each patch becomes a numerical token, and self-attention helps the model combine information from different image regions. A CNN instead starts with local convolution filters that learn edges and patterns before gradually building larger features. For example, recognizing a vehicle may require linking its wheels and windows. Both designs can learn these relationships, but their starting operations differ.
questions.figure:
01 · VISUAL LESSON

ViT sees patch tokens; a CNN learns with local filters

Both can classify images. Original ViT is patch-based and uses global self-attention; CNNs build visual features through local convolution filters. Neither is universally better.

questions.stem: How does ViT convert an image into patch embeddings, and how many patch tokens come from a 224×224 RGB image using 16×16 patches?
options: ViT divides the image into 16×16 pixel patches, producing 196 patches, then keeps all 768 raw RGB values as final learned embeddings without projection. A classification token replaces one image patch, so the encoder sees 196 total tokens.

ViT cuts a 224×224 RGB image into 14 patches total, each containing 16×16×3 values. It learns one shared vector for the complete image and duplicates it across the sequence, giving 14 patch tokens after projection.

ViT forms a grid of 196 patches from the image but encodes each patch as three separate color tokens. This gives 588 patch tokens before adding any classification token, while projection changes the count of tokens rather than vector size.

ViT makes a 14×14 grid of 16×16 patches, giving 196 patch tokens. Each RGB patch has 768 raw values that a learned projection maps to the model's embedding size; a common classifier adds one separate [CLS] token.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A 224×224 image divided into 16-pixel patches has 14 patches across and 14 down, so it produces 196 patches. Each RGB patch contains 16×16×3 = 768 pixel values. A learned linear projection turns these raw values into a vector of the model's chosen embedding size. Some classifiers add one [CLS] token, making 197 tokens in total. Imagine cutting a satellite photo into tiles: each tile becomes a compact learned description, not a separate final label.
questions.figure:
02 · VISUAL LESSON

224×224 image → 196 patches → learned vectors

The 768 raw pixel values are projected to model embedding size D (not necessarily 768). Example: ViT-B/16 uses 196 patches and one [CLS] token at 224×224 resolution.

questions.stem: Why do Vision Transformers use positional embeddings and sometimes a [CLS] token, and how do these affect image classification?
options: Positional embeddings encode where patches belong in an image grid. A learned [CLS] token can gather information through the encoder for classification, while some ViT variants instead classify by pooling patch features.

Positional embeddings store the category predicted for each patch, allowing ViT to classify images without attention. The [CLS] token encodes the original pixel dimensions and is removed before the encoder processes the token sequence.

Positional embeddings tell ViT where patches occur, but each position receives the same vector so absolute order is ignored. The [CLS] token determines which patches are visible and blocks attention between distant image regions.

Positional embeddings assign individual pixel coordinates to every color channel within a patch, while the [CLS] token is an image label supplied during training. Together they replace the model's learned classifier weights and pooling operations.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Patch tokens describe image content, but without added position information the original ViT encoder cannot reliably distinguish where those patches came from. Positional embeddings supply location information. In a common classification design, a learned [CLS] token joins the sequence; after attention layers, its final representation is passed to a classifier. Some variants instead pool patch tokens. Consider a face: the positions of eyes and mouth matter, not merely which features appear somewhere in the photo.
questions.figure:
03 · VISUAL LESSON

Position tells ViT where a patch belongs

Patch embeddings represent appearance; positional embeddings encode locations. The common classification design reads a learned [CLS] token after the encoder; other variants use pooled patch features.

questions.stem: How do multi-head self-attention, query-key-value projections, residual connections, and MLP layers work together inside a ViT encoder?
options: ViT uses query, key, and value projections to choose one neighboring patch for every token, then copies its features without mixing scores. Each head covers the same fixed region; residual connections replace the tokens with MLP outputs afterward.

ViT creates query, key, and value vectors, but attention weights are computed by comparing values directly rather than queries with keys. Multi-head attention then averages class labels, and the MLP updates only the final [CLS] token.

ViT projects tokens into queries, keys, and values, then uses scaled query-key scores to weight values through softmax. Different heads learn distinct links; residual paths, normalization, and MLP layers refine token representations.

ViT compares query and key scores across all patches, but multiplies the scores by keys to produce new values. The MLP creates position vectors before attention and residual connections prevent earlier patch information from reaching later encoder layers.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Each ViT token is transformed into query, key, and value vectors. A token's query is compared with other keys; scaled scores go through softmax and become weights for combining values. Several attention heads can learn different relationships. The combined result is projected, then residual connections and normalization help keep learning stable. An MLP further transforms each token. Imagine inspecting a painting: one head may connect matching colors while another connects related object parts. The diagrams show simplified, illustrative weights.
questions.figure:
04 · VISUAL LESSON

Attention: each patch can mix information from others

Heatmaps are illustrative attention weights, not measured values. Multiple heads can emphasize different relationships; residual paths, normalization and the MLP refine tokens after attention.

questions.stem: How can PyTorch create ViT patch embeddings, prepend a learnable [CLS] token, and add positional embeddings to prepare the Transformer input?
options: PyTorch can extract image patches and project them to vectors, but should append one [CLS] token for every patch. Position vectors are added only after the classifier so the encoder learns image location entirely from attention scores.

PyTorch can extract fixed-size patches, project their flattened RGB values into token vectors, prepend one learnable [CLS] token, then add positional embeddings with matching sequence length and feature size before passing tokens into an encoder.

PyTorch can reshape an image into patches, but must average those patches into one vector before adding the [CLS] token. Position embeddings then replace the patch content because each token already contains enough visual information for classification.

PyTorch can project every patch to a feature vector and add position embeddings, but the [CLS] token should be initialized from the model's predicted label. Token features are sorted by confidence before they enter the Transformer encoder.
questions.explanation: Explanation: First, PyTorch cuts an RGB tensor into equal patches. A learned layer maps each flattened patch into a vector with the same embedding dimension. Next, one learnable [CLS] token is placed at the beginning, and position vectors are added to all tokens. For a 32×32 image with 8×8 patches, there are 16 patch tokens plus one [CLS], producing 17 token vectors. The code below demonstrates these shapes with random parameters; it does not perform attention or classify an image.
questions.figure:
05 · VISUAL LESSON

A minimal, runnable ViT token-preparation example

Python · PyTorch patch tokens 12 lines · runnable · no downloaded weights
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn.functional import unfold
torch.manual_seed(7)
image = torch.rand(1, 3, 32, 32)
patches = unfold(image, 8, stride=8).transpose(1, 2)
embed = nn.Linear(3 * 8 * 8, 64)(patches)
cls = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, 1, 64))
pos = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, 17, 64) * 0.02)
tokens = torch.cat([cls.expand(1, -1, -1), embed], 1)
tokens = tokens + pos
print(patches.shape, tokens.shape)

Expected output: torch.Size([1, 16, 192]) torch.Size([1, 17, 64]). The parameters here are freshly initialized.

Expected patch tensor: [1, 16, 192]. With a class token, the input sequence is [1, 17, 64]. These are untrained embeddings; this example does not perform attention or classification.

questions.stem: Why are pretraining, transfer learning, data augmentation, and careful fine-tuning important for Vision Transformers when labeled image datasets are limited?
options: Pretraining lets ViT learn transferable features, but fine-tuning must replace all token embeddings with random weights because previous position information cannot adapt. Augmentation should also be applied to test images to ensure identical training conditions.

ViT may benefit from pretrained features, but augmentations mainly increase class counts instead of image variety. Fine-tuning should select model settings on the held-out test set, since testing many configurations gives the fairest estimate of performance.

ViT pretraining learns general patterns, but a small labeled dataset should usually train a new full Transformer from scratch before freezing its attention layers. Augmentation is unnecessary when pretrained weights are available and class labels are accurate.

Pretraining can give ViT broadly useful visual features before a smaller labeled task. Fine-tuning adapts weights or a task head, while training-only augmentation and regularization improve robustness; separate validation and test splits check generalization.
questions.explanation: Explanation: ViT models may need substantial data or strong training recipes to learn useful visual patterns from scratch. Pretraining provides a starting representation, and transfer learning adapts it to a smaller labeled task. For example, a leaf-disease classifier can begin with general visual features, then learn disease-specific patterns from local field photos. Apply appropriate augmentation to training images, not to the final test set, and use validation data for tuning. Pretraining helps but does not guarantee success under domain shift.
questions.figure:
06 · VISUAL LESSON

Pretraining learns general patterns; fine-tuning adapts them

Using pretrained weights often helps when labeled data are scarce. Fine-tune only on the training split, use task-appropriate augmentation, and evaluate on untouched held-out data.

questions.stem: What limitations appear when ViTs process high-resolution images, and how do patch size, attention cost, efficient architectures, and deployment testing affect their use in detection and segmentation?
options: High-resolution images create more patches, but attention memory stays almost constant because softmax is calculated separately for each token. Increasing patch size always improves small-object boundaries, and classification tokens directly provide pixel masks for segmentation.

High-resolution ViTs require more patches, but their attention cost rises only linearly with patch count. Windowed attention removes the need for cross-window information, and pretrained classification heads can directly localize objects without downstream adaptation.

High-resolution images produce more patch tokens, and full attention forms roughly quadratic token-pair scores. Larger patches reduce cost but may lose detail; efficient or hierarchical designs plus task-specific heads and real-device evaluation help detection and segmentation.

High-resolution ViTs create longer token sequences, but shrinking patch size reduces computation because each token holds fewer pixels. Detection and segmentation need only different labels for the [CLS] token, so spatial decoding and boundary evaluation are unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Explanation: For fixed 16×16 patches, a 224×224 image has 196 image tokens; a 448×448 image has 784. Full attention compares token pairs, growing from 196² = 38,416 to 784² = 614,656, sixteen times as many scores. Larger patches lower this cost but can hide small details. Windowed or hierarchical attention can help, while detection and segmentation require spatial features and task-specific heads. On real hardware, evaluate latency, memory, small-object accuracy, and mask boundaries. The figure omits [CLS] for simple arithmetic.

Counts exclude any [CLS] token for easier comparison. Attention score storage grows roughly with N²; efficient attention, windows, hierarchical stages and careful resolution choices can reduce costs.
